alg-functions: A function gives each input one output, written f(input) = output . The domain is every allowed input (no zero denominators, no square roots of negatives); the range is every output. Zeros are inputs with output 0 ; the y -intercept is (0, f(0)) . Piecewise-defined functions use the piece whose condition the input meets.
alg-intervals: Interval notation writes a stretch of the number line with its two ends: brackets for included ends, parentheses for excluded ends and for ±∞ , and ∪ to join pieces. Solve linear inequalities like equations, flipping the sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative, and check one value.
change-in-tandem: Two quantities that change together are described by direction and by how fast. A function is increasing on an interval when larger inputs give larger outputs, decreasing when they give smaller ones. Its rate of change says how fast the output moves; when the rate of change increases the graph is concave up, and when it decreases the graph is concave down.
alg-lines: Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x , the same between any two points of a line. Point-slope form y − y_1 = m(x − x_1) builds a line from one point and the slope, and y = y_1 + m(x − x_1) gives its value at any x . In context, slope is output units per input unit.
rates-of-change: The average rate of change of f on [a, b] is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) , the slope of the line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) , in output units per input unit. Over a short interval around a point it estimates how fast f changes at that point, and comparing those estimates tells where f changes faster.
alg-quadratics: A quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c graphs as a parabola with its vertex at x = −b/2a . Solve f(x) = 0 by factors, by square roots or by the quadratic formula; the discriminant b² − 4ac counts the real zeros. Completing the square gives vertex form a(x − h)² + k , which shows the vertex (h, k) .
linear-quadratic-rates: A linear function has one rate of change. A quadratic's average rates over consecutive equal intervals change by a constant amount, so its second differences are constant; increasing rates mean concave up, decreasing rates concave down. The average rate of change on [a, b] is the slope of the secant line, and a secant estimate is too big where the graph is concave up and too small where it is concave down.
alg-polynomial-algebra: Multiply polynomials by distributing every term and combining like terms. Factor by taking out a common factor first, then using a difference of squares a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) , a sum or difference of cubes, or grouping. A product equals 0 when a factor does, and p(a) = 0 means x − a is a factor.
polynomial-rates: A polynomial function has a degree and a leading term. Where it switches between increasing and decreasing it has a local maximum or minimum; on a closed interval the endpoints count too, and the greatest and least of all these values are the global maximum and minimum. Where its rate of change switches between increasing and decreasing, the graph has a point of inflection.
alg-complex-numbers: The imaginary unit i has i² = −1 , so √(−b²) = bi . Complex numbers a + bi add and multiply like binomials, with i² replaced by −1 . A quadratic with real coefficients and a negative discriminant has two complex solutions that are complex conjugates, a ± bi .
complex-zeros: Each factor (x − a)^k of a polynomial gives a zero a of multiplicity k : the graph crosses at odd multiplicity and touches at even multiplicity. A polynomial of degree n has n complex zeros counting multiplicity, and with real coefficients the non-real ones come in conjugate pairs. Constant n th differences point to degree n ; even and odd functions show mirror symmetry.
polynomial-end-behavior: As |x| grows, a polynomial behaves like its leading term a_nx^n . Even degree sends both ends the same way and odd degree sends them opposite ways; the sign of a_n picks the direction. State end behavior in full limit notation, for example lim as x → −∞, p(x) = ∞ and lim as x → ∞, p(x) = −∞ .
alg-rational-expressions: A rational expression is a quotient of polynomials, undefined where its denominator is 0 . Factor, then cancel common factors only, keeping the original exclusions. Add with a common denominator, multiply across, divide by the reciprocal, and split a sum in the numerator term by term.
rational-end-behavior: A rational function's end behavior matches the quotient of its leading terms. Equal degrees give a horizontal asymptote at the ratio of the leading coefficients; a larger denominator degree gives y = 0 ; a numerator one degree larger gives a slant asymptote. State the end behavior in limit notation, such as lim as x → ∞, r(x) = 3 .
rational-zeros: The real zeros of a rational function are the numerator's zeros that are in its domain. Zeros and excluded inputs split the number line; a test value in each interval gives the sign there. Solve a rational inequality from that sign chart, including zeros only for ≤ or ≥ and never an excluded input.
vertical-asymptotes: A rational function has a vertical asymptote x = a where (x − a) divides the denominator more times than the numerator. Describe it from each side with one-sided limits, lim as x → a⁻, f(x) and lim as x → a⁺, f(x) , each ∞ or −∞ , found from the signs of the factors just beside a .
rational-holes: A rational function has a hole at x = a when (x − a) divides the numerator at least as often as the denominator. Cancel the factor and evaluate at a to get the hole's height L ; then lim as x → a, r(x) = L while r(a) is undefined. Near a hole the outputs approach a number, unlike near a vertical asymptote.
equivalent-representations: Factored form shows zeros, holes, vertical asymptotes and the domain; standard form shows end behavior; division writes a rational function as quotient plus remainder over divisor, and a linear quotient is the slant asymptote. Pascal's triangle expands (a + b)^n .
transformations: g(x) = af(b(x − h)) + k dilates and reflects f by a and b and translates it h right and k up. Outside changes act on outputs and the range; inside changes act on inputs and the domain, in reverse.
model-selection: Choose a model type from the changes over equal input steps and from the context, then state the domain and range the context allows and the assumptions the model makes.
alg-systems: Solve a system by substitution or elimination, removing one variable at a time. Fitting a model through data points means writing one equation per point and solving for the constants, stored at full precision.
model-construction: Build a model from data points (a system), from features and transformations, or by regression; store its constants; use it to predict and to find average rates of change with units, only for inputs the context allows.
alg-exponents: Same base: add exponents to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply exponents for a power of a power. b^(−n) is a reciprocal and b^(m/n) is a root then a power. Writing both sides with one base turns 4^x = 32 into 2x = 5 .
sequences: Arithmetic sequences add a common difference: a_n = a_k + d(n − k) . Geometric sequences multiply by a common ratio: g_n = g_kr^(n − k) . Equal amounts versus multiplied amounts is the difference that grows into linear versus exponential change.
linear-vs-exponential: Over equal-length input intervals, a linear function adds a constant difference and an exponential function multiplies by a constant ratio. Justify a model type with both halves and the numbers; with unequal steps, compare rates or per-unit ratios instead.
exponential-functions: f(x) = ab^x is monotonic with one concavity and a horizontal asymptote, written in limit notation. The base is the growth factor ( 1 + the percent change as a decimal). Adding k moves the asymptote to y = k ; the natural base e is one choice of b .
exponential-manipulation: Exponent rules rewrite exponential functions: b^(x + k) = b^kb^x (a horizontal shift is a vertical dilation), b^cx = (b^c)^x (a horizontal dilation is a new base) and b^(−x) = (1/b)^x . Equivalent forms make different features easy to read.
exponential-modeling: Build ab^t from an initial value and a ratio, from two points, or by exponential regression. The base is the growth factor; rewrite it for other time units with rational exponents. Predict and solve with the stored model, and only where the context and data allow.
model-validation: Residuals (actual minus predicted) measure how far a model misses each data point. Choose the model whose residuals are small and patternless, and read the sign of the residuals to say where a model underestimates or overestimates.
composition: A composite function chains two functions: f(g(x)) puts the output of g into f . Evaluate from the inside out and show the inner value. The order matters, the domain is the inputs whose inner outputs f can take, and the identity function I(x) = x leaves any function unchanged. You can compose from tables, graphs or formulas, and take a function apart into an inner and an outer step.
inverse-functions: An inverse function undoes a function: f⁻¹(b) = a exactly when f(a) = b . It exists when no output repeats, which you justify with specific values, or after restricting the domain. Find it from a table by swapping rows, from a graph by reflecting across y = x , and from a formula by swapping x and y and solving. Composing a function with its inverse gives the identity.
logarithmic-expressions: A logarithm is an exponent: log_b c = a means b^a = c . The common logarithm uses base 10 and the natural logarithm uses base e . Find exact values by writing the input as a power of the base, and estimate others between consecutive powers. Logarithms take only positive inputs. A logarithmic scale spaces numbers by their logarithms, so equal steps are equal factors.
exp-log-inverses: With the same base, f(x) = b^x and g(x) = log_b x are inverses: each undoes the other, their graphs reflect across y = x , and their domains, ranges and asymptotes trade places. Adding to the input of an exponential multiplies its output; multiplying the input of a logarithm adds to its output. To invert a stretched exponential, undo the outer steps first, then take the logarithm.
logarithmic-functions: A logarithmic function f(x) = alog_b x is defined only for x > 0 , with a vertical asymptote at x = 0 . With a > 0 and b > 1 it is increasing and concave down, so its rate of change decreases: lim as x → 0⁺, f(x) = −∞ and lim as x → ∞, f(x) = ∞ , with no extrema. Shifts move the asymptote and the domain. Describe asymptote behavior in limit notation from the side where f is defined.
logarithmic-manipulation: Logarithms turn products into sums, quotients into differences and powers into multiples, because exponents behave that way. Change of base writes any logarithm as a multiple of another, so every logarithmic function is a vertical dilation of every other. On graphs, multiplying the input shifts the graph up or down. Each rule needs positive inputs; watch for domain changes such as ln (x²) versus 2ln x .
exp-log-equations: To solve an exponential equation, isolate the power and use a common base or a logarithm. To solve a logarithmic equation, combine into one logarithm and rewrite as a power, then check for extraneous solutions. An equation quadratic in e^x is solved with u = e^x , rejecting roots where e^x would not be positive. Inequalities keep their direction for bases above 1 and flip for bases between 0 and 1 .
logarithmic-modeling: Use a logarithmic model y = a + bln x when the input must multiply by a constant for the output to rise by a constant. Build it from two points or by logarithmic regression, keeping the constants stored. Predict outputs by substituting and find inputs by rewriting as a power. The model is concave down, so its rate of change decreases; it is supported only near the data and fails near x = 0 .
semi-log-plots: A semi-log plot puts one axis on a logarithmic scale. Exponential data y = a⋅b^x then fall on a straight line, because log y = log a + xlog b . The slope of the line is log b and its intercept is log a , so you can read the model's growth factor and starting value from the line. Linear data, or exponential data with a vertical shift, bend instead.
periodic-phenomena: A periodic function repeats its outputs every P units of input, f(x + P) = f(x) , and the smallest such P is the period. Learn one cycle and you know the function everywhere: shift any input by whole periods into the cycle. Increasing and decreasing intervals, concavity and rates of change repeat every period, and the average rate of change over a full period is 0 .
alg-right-triangle: In a right triangle, name the legs from the angle θ : opposite and adjacent. Then sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse , cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent . The ratios depend only on the angle, so one angle and one side are enough to find the other sides.
alg-circles: The 45-45-90 triangle has sides 1:1:√2 and the 30-60-90 triangle 1:√3:2 ; they give exact sines and cosines at 30^(∘) , 45^(∘) and 60^(∘) . An arc cut off by a central angle of θ degrees is the fraction θ/360 of the circumference 2πr . The circle with center (h, k) and radius r is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² .
sine-cosine-tangent: An angle in radians is arc length over radius, so a full turn is 2π . Place the angle θ in standard position; its terminal ray meets the unit circle at (cos θ, sin θ) , and tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) is the ray's slope. These definitions work for every angle, and the quadrant sets the signs.
sine-cosine-values: Exact sines and cosines at multiples of π/6 and π/4 come from the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles. Find the reference angle, use its first-quadrant value, and give it the sign of the quadrant. On a circle of radius r , the point at angle θ is (rcos θ, rsin θ) .
sine-cosine-curves: The graph of y = sin θ is the height of the point at angle θ on the unit circle; y = cos θ is its horizontal position. Both repeat every 2π and stay between −1 and 1 , and cosine is sine shifted π/2 to the left. Each graph is concave down above the axis and concave up below it, steepest at its zeros and flat at its highest and lowest points.
sinusoidal-functions: A sinusoidal function is a sine or cosine graph after dilations and translations. Four numbers describe it: the midline y = (max + min)/2 , the amplitude (max − min)/2 , the period (the length of one cycle) and the frequency, one over the period. Sine is odd and cosine is even.
sinusoidal-transformations: In f(θ) = asin (b(θ + c)) + d , |a| is the amplitude, 2π/(|b|) the period, c the phase shift (left by c ) and y = d the midline; cosine works the same way. To build a formula from a graph, read d and |a| , get b = 2π/period , then find c from a landmark point. Factor out b before reading a shift.
sinusoidal-modeling: To model a periodic context, get the midline and amplitude from the greatest and least values, the period (and b = 2π/period ) from the cycle length or frequency, and the shift from one landmark time. With data, sinusoidal regression does the same job. Use the model on the domain the context supports, and describe change on an interval as two statements: the direction of the quantity and the direction of its rate of change.
tangent-function: tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) , the slope of the terminal ray. It is 0 at θ = kπ , has vertical asymptotes at θ = π/2 + kπ with outputs growing without bound on each side, and has period π . For atan (b(x − c)) + d the period is π/(|b|) and the asymptotes shift with the graph.
inverse-trig: Restricted to [−π/2 , π/2] , [0, π] and (−π/2 , π/2) , sine, cosine and tangent are invertible. sin⁻¹ , cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ take a ratio and return the one angle in that interval. Inverse is not reciprocal, and sin⁻¹ (sin x) = x only for x in the restricted interval.
trig-equations: To solve a trigonometric equation, isolate the function, take the principal value with the inverse, find the second angle by symmetry, then add periods until you have every solution in the interval and none outside it. Inequalities follow the equation: its solutions cut the interval into pieces, and a test value decides each piece.
sec-csc-cot: sec x = 1/(cos x) , csc x = 1/(sin x) and cot x = (cos x)/(sin x) . Each has vertical asymptotes where its denominator is 0 . Secant and cosecant equal their partners at ±1 and never take values strictly between −1 and 1 ; cotangent takes every real value and has period π .
trig-identities: The Pythagorean identity sin² x + cos² x = 1 and its forms with tan , sec , cot and csc ; the sum and difference identities for sine and cosine; and the double-angle identities sin (2x) = 2sin xcos x and cos (2x) = cos² x − sin² x = 2cos² x − 1 = 1 − 2sin² x . Use them to find exact values, to rewrite expressions as one function, and to solve equations.
polar-coordinates: A point in polar coordinates (r, θ) is r units from the pole in the direction θ . Convert with x = rcos θ , y = rsin θ , r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x , checking the quadrant. Every point has many polar names, and a complex number a + bi can be written as r(cos θ + isin θ) .
polar-curves: A polar function r = f(θ) assigns a signed distance to every direction. Read it from its graph of r against θ : zeros are visits to the pole, negative values are drawn on the opposite ray, and each hump draws a petal or loop. Circles ( r = a , r = acos θ ), limaçons and cardioids ( r = a + bcos θ ) and roses ( r = asin (nθ) ) are the families to know.
polar-rates: For a polar function, the average rate of change of r on [a, b] is (r(b) − r(a))/(b − a) units per radian, the slope of a secant line on the graph of r against θ . The distance from the origin is |r| : it increases where r is positive and increasing or negative and decreasing, and decreases in the other two cases. Extremes of |r| give the farthest and closest points.
parametric-functions: A parametric function f(t) = (x(t), y(t)) sends each value of the parameter t to a point. As t increases the points trace a curve with a direction. The curve is drawn in the xy -plane, and it need not be the graph of a function of x .
parametric-motion: A particle moving in the plane has position (x(t), y(t)) at time t . Where x(t) increases it moves right, where y(t) increases it moves up, and the turning points of each coordinate give the farthest right, left, highest and lowest positions. Read each coordinate separately, then put the two together.
parametric-rates: For a parametric function on [t_1, t_2] , the average rates of change of x(t) and y(t) say how fast each coordinate changed per unit of t . Their quotient, the change in y over the change in x , is the slope of the segment joining the two points, an average steepness of the path.
parametric-circles-lines: (h + rcos t, k + rsin t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π traces the circle with center (h, k) and radius r once counterclockwise, starting at (h + r, k) . A segment from P to Q is P + (Q − P)t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 , coordinate by coordinate. Both describe not only a set of points but a trip along it.
implicit-functions: An implicitly defined function is an equation linking x and y ; its graph is every solution point. Substitute a value to find points, count the y -values for one x to decide whether the curve is a function of x , and solve for y to split it into functions.
conic-sections: Conic sections are the parabola, the ellipse and the hyperbola, all implicitly defined curves. In standard form you read off the center or vertex, the distances a and b from the denominators' square roots, and for a hyperbola the asymptotes y − k = ±b/a (x − h) . The signs of the squared terms tell which conic you have.
parametrizing-implicit: To parametrize a curve given by an equation, choose x(t) and y(t) that make the equation true for every t : (t, f(t)) for a graph, (h + acos t, k + bsin t) for an ellipse, (h + asec t, k + btan t) for a hyperbola. To go back, solve for the trig functions and use a Pythagorean identity.
vectors: A vector ⟨a, b⟩ is a size and a direction: a across, b up, length √(a² + b²) . Vectors add tip to tail (component by component), scale by numbers, and give a unit vector when divided by their length. The dot product ac + bd measures the angle between two vectors and is 0 for perpendicular ones.
vector-valued-functions: A vector-valued function p(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ is a parametric function written as position vectors. The displacement p(t_2) − p(t_1) says how far and which way the object moved, and dividing by t_2 − t_1 gives the average rate of change vector, made of the average rates of x and y .
matrices: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers with dimensions rows by columns. Matrices of the same size add entry by entry. A product AB is defined when A has as many columns as B has rows; each entry is a row of A times a column of B . The order of the factors matters.
inverse-determinant: For a 2×2 matrix the determinant ad − bc is the signed area of the parallelogram made by its columns. If it is not 0 , the inverse is 1/(ad − bc) [d, −b; −c, a] , which undoes the matrix and solves AX = B as X = A⁻¹B . If it is 0 , there is no inverse.
linear-transformations: A linear transformation sends ⟨x, y⟩ to ⟨ax + by, cx + dy⟩ , which is the matrix [a, b; c, d] times the input. Its columns are the images of ⟨1, 0⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩ . Rotations, reflections, dilations and shears are all linear, and every area is multiplied by the absolute value of the determinant.
matrices-as-functions: A matrix is a function on vectors. Doing B and then A is the single matrix AB , read right to left, and repeating A gives A^n . When det A ≠ 0 , A⁻¹ undoes A and recovers an input from its output; when det A = 0 , two inputs share an output and nothing can undo it.
matrix-modeling: A transition matrix holds the chances of moving between states in one step, with "from" columns that add up to 1. Multiplying a state vector by T moves it one step forward, T^n moves it n steps, T⁻¹ moves it one step back, and a steady state is a vector that T leaves unchanged.
